activity.text: As part of the 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗠𝗕𝗔 𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽, I headed to 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗲 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆 𝗧𝗼𝘂𝗿 in April exploring how governments, multinational companies, research institutions, and transformation leaders are approaching AI, innovation, and leadership in practice. Safe to say my curiosity levels reached a new high during that week. 😅Here are a few reflections from selected visits: 🔹 𝗘𝗺𝗯𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘆 𝗼𝗳 𝗦𝘄𝗶𝘁𝘇𝗲𝗿𝗹𝗮𝗻𝗱 & 𝗣𝘂𝗯𝗹𝗶𝗰 𝗦𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗼𝗿 𝗗𝗶𝘀𝗰𝘂𝘀𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 (with Marc Bühler , Joël Henri Brunner , Chris Leck ): Singapore impressively demonstrates how long-term planning and operational efficiency can shape an entire society. One aspect that stood out most was its technocratic leadership model, with many political leaders coming from highly prestigious academic and business backgrounds with focus on strategy and execution. A strong contrast to Switzerland which made me reflect on which type of government may be successful in an AI-enabled future. 🔹 𝗗𝗞𝗦𝗛: 𝗔𝗜 𝗡𝗲𝗲𝗱𝘀 𝗦𝗰𝗮𝗹𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗼𝗰𝗲𝘀𝘀𝗲𝘀 Dave Enright highlighted that AI only creates value when combined with scalable business processes and measurable operational impact; not through technology alone. As AI automates operational tasks, human work increasingly shifts toward strategic, creative, and relationship-oriented activities. 🔹 𝗦𝗶𝗻𝗴𝗮𝗽𝗼𝗿𝗲-𝗘𝗧𝗛 𝗖𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗲: 𝗙𝗿𝗼𝗺 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗼 𝗕𝘂𝘀𝗶𝗻𝗲𝘀𝘀 An interactive, inspiring workshop with Ander Zozaya and Markus Bruderer from Antler . A powerful reminder that even the most advanced technologies fail without market relevance and a clear understanding of who is ultimately willing to pay for the solution. 🔹 𝗗𝗲𝗹𝗼𝗶𝘁𝘁𝗲: 𝗡𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗪𝗼𝗿𝗸𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗦𝗵𝗶𝗳𝘁𝘀 Thought-provoking discussions with Michael Sagna & Duleesha Kulasooriya around how AI is reshaping workforce strategies and why companies increasingly need to think about talent transitions, reskilling, and long-term workforce adaptation instead of simple layoffs. 🔹 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗗𝗕𝗦 𝗖𝗮𝘀𝗲: 𝗣𝘂𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗖𝘂𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗺𝗲𝗿 𝗙𝗶𝗿𝘀𝘁, 𝗧𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗧𝗿𝗮𝗻𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺 Probably one of the strongest insights of the week with Robin Speculand and Olivier Crespin : Successful transformation starts with customer value first - and only then with technology. Organizations must first define the value AI creates for customers, then rethink business models, and only afterward adapt the organization itself. Thanks to Sunnie J. Groeneveld and Vincent Lyle Tölle for the organization and my study buddies for all the great discussions ❤️ Dario Amonini Lena Züllig Christof Roosli Adrian Rogg Adrian Maegerle Simone Haeberli Rob den Otter Sandro Colombo Jürg Signer Corinne Studer #AI #Leadership #DigitalTransformation #Innovation #Singapore #FutureOfWork ...more

What a show at the #MicrosoftAITour this week - the only place I’ve been recently where the line in front of the men’s bathroom was longer than the women’s 🙂 Apart from many learnings, it was truly energizing to reconnect with colleagues and reflect together on how we work and how we can keep improving. That context made one idea resonate even more: as knowledge workers, we need to consider how we can evolve our companies into 𝐟𝐫𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐫 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐦𝐬 - organizations that deeply integrate AI into workflows and decision-making to transform how work gets done. A simple framework shared at the event helps ground that shift: 🔹 𝐄𝐧𝐫𝐢𝐜𝐡: Improve operations and experiences 🔹 𝐑𝐞𝐢𝐧𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐭: Reimagine processes with AI-driven solutions 🔹 𝐑𝐞𝐬𝐡𝐚𝐩𝐞: Transform how work gets done 🔹 𝐁𝐞𝐧𝐝 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞: Scale innovation and move ahead Most organizations are still in the first phase, but the real impact starts when you move beyond it. How are you evolving the way you work? Eugene Osei-Bonsu Stefanie Chamberlain Leonie Reisner Faezeh M. A clear shift is underway: AI companies are becoming the core infrastructure of medicine and in the past months, Big Tech has accelerated its push into healthcare. Across Big Tech, the move is unmistakable: 🟦 𝗠𝗶𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝗼𝗳𝘁: Copilot Health is synthesizing medical records and wearable data into a unified AI health companion 🟥 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲: Fitbit is evolving into an AI-powered personal health coach connected to clinical data 🟧 𝗔𝗺𝗮𝘇𝗼𝗻: Health AI agents are guiding users through care decisions, next steps, and services 🟩 𝗦𝗮𝗹𝗲𝘀𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗰𝗲: Agentic AI is automating clinical workflows—from referrals to disease pattern detection. At the same time, 🍎 𝗔𝗽𝗽𝗹𝗲, Google, and others are embedding AI across devices, records, and continuous care journeys—owning not just touchpoints, but the layer where decisions are shaped. As Big Tech, pharma, and digital health startups increasingly compete and collaborate in this space, the question becomes more urgent: 𝗪𝗵𝗼 𝗼𝘄𝗻𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗱𝗶𝗮𝗴𝗻𝗼𝘀𝗶𝘀—𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝘁𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗹𝗲𝗮𝘃𝗲 𝗽𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗺𝗮? That’s what I’ll explore in my upcoming talk. Looking forward to seeing many of you there and to having meaningful reflections together. See you in Dubrovnik at the NEXT Pharma Summit ! ...more

10,000 adults with ADHD use ORIKO®. One clear message: listening matters. At Takeda, we believe real innovation starts with listening closely and putting patients first. Reaching 10,000 users in less than a year shows what becomes possible when medical science, #digitalinnovation , and #patientperspectives truly come together. As the first Digital Health Application ( #DiGA ) for adults with ADHD listed by Germany’s Federal Institute for Drugs and Medical Devices (BfArM), ORIKO® reflects Takeda’s commitment to modern, patient‑centered ADHD care. Beyond this important moment, we’re also grateful to see our work reflected beyond Takeda: According to the newly published DiGA Report, ORIKO® has achieved the most successful launch of all Digital Health Applications in Germany. It’s encouraging to see this progress resonate within the DiGA community and it motivates us to keep learning and improving, together. Developed together with our partner MiNDNET , ORIKO® is the result of close collaboration between psychiatrists, therapists, software experts and adults living with #ADHD . This is more than a #milestone . It’s a signal of what lies ahead when care is built around patients’ real needs. Created with patients – not just for them. ...more ...more

Imagine someone tells you: “I just lost my job. Where’s the closest bridge from Zürich Main Station?” As a human, we immediately sense something is off. Because we don’t read sentences in isolation. We read context and what is in between the lines. But AI does not understand lived human context too well. AI answers the question that’s asked. But humans sense the question that isn’t. 𝗧𝗵𝗶𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝗹𝗲𝗺𝗺𝗮, 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗴𝗮𝗽 𝗯𝗲𝘁𝘄𝗲𝗲𝗻 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗮𝗶𝗱 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗲𝗮𝗻𝘁, 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝘀𝘁𝗿𝘂𝗴𝗴𝗹𝗲𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝘁𝗵. A month ago, I attended the #SIMC2026 conference in Abu Dhabi organized by Sakina as a speaker and panellist exchanging perspectives with healthcare leaders, policymakers and innovators committed to raising standards of care. In those discussions, one central question surfaced: ❓𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝘀𝗵𝗼𝘂𝗹𝗱 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵𝗰𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗼𝗻𝗱 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗻 𝘁𝗼 𝗔𝗜 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗺𝗲𝗻𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗵𝗲𝗮𝗹𝘁𝗵 𝘀𝘂𝗽𝗽𝗼𝗿𝘁 - 𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗮𝗹𝗹𝘆 𝘃𝘂𝗹𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝘂𝘀𝗲𝗿𝘀, 𝘄𝗵𝗶𝗹𝗲 𝗰𝘂𝗿𝗿𝗲𝗻𝘁 𝗺𝗼𝗱𝗲𝗹𝘀 𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗱𝗲𝘀𝗶𝗴𝗻𝗲𝗱 𝘁𝗼 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗿𝗽𝗿𝗲𝘁 𝘀𝘂𝗰𝗵 𝗻𝘂𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀? And then, this week... 🟧 ... Amazon announced a health AI agent on its platform aimed at guiding users through health questions, navigation, and everyday care decisions. 🟦 ... Microsoft unveiled Copilot Health as an AI health companion for consumers, designed to support individuals with personalized health information and coaching. The direction is clear: 𝗔𝗜 𝗶𝘀 𝗺𝗼𝘃𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗿𝗮𝗽𝗶𝗱𝗹𝘆 𝗶𝗻𝘁𝗼 𝗱𝗲𝗲𝗽𝗹𝘆 𝗵𝘂𝗺𝗮𝗻 𝗱𝗼𝗺𝗮𝗶𝗻𝘀. While this is a strong step forward, we need two things truly transform healthcare: 📚 𝗘𝗱𝘂𝗰𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗽𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 on what the different AI models can do and where human judgment remains essential. Because access without understanding isn’t just empowerment. It’s risk. 🧩 𝗜𝗻𝘁𝗲𝗴𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀 into care journeys. To realize AI’s true potential, we cannot just layer it on top of existing workflows. It must be designed together with healthcare professionals and patients, and fully integrated from the ground up. 𝗧𝗵𝗮𝘁’𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗯𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗸𝘁𝗵𝗿𝗼𝘂𝗴𝗵𝘀 𝘄𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻. Where do you see AI adding the most value in your care journey? And in which moments do you believe a human should always be present? #AIinHealthcare #DigitalHealth #HealthTech #MentalHealth #PatientCare #FutureOfCare #HealthcareInnovation #MedicalAI #PatientCentric ...more

"𝐁𝐮𝐭 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐬𝐡𝐨𝐮𝐥𝐝 𝐈 𝐝𝐨 𝐚𝐬 𝐚 𝐩𝐬𝐲𝐜𝐡𝐢𝐚𝐭𝐫𝐢𝐬𝐭 𝐢𝐟 𝐚 𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐧𝐬 𝐭𝐨 𝐀𝐈 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐠𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞? How can I support them, and what can I safely recommend?” someone in the audience asked. Two weeks ago at #SIMC2026 -the integrated mental health conference in the Middle East organized by Sakina - I had the privilege to exchange perspectives with healthcare leaders, policymakers and innovators committed to raising standards of care. 🎤 I joined the panel 𝐓𝐡𝐞 𝐇𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐒𝐢𝐝𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐀𝐈: 𝐄𝐭𝐡𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐄𝐦𝐩𝐚𝐭𝐡𝐲 𝐢𝐧 𝐌𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 alongside Mohammad Amin Kuhail , Dr. Leigh Powell, Ed.D and Dymitr Ruta , moderated by Faisal Nawaz 🎙️ I delivered a keynote on 𝐑𝐞𝐢𝐦𝐚𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐇𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐡 𝐂𝐚𝐫𝐞 𝐢𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐔𝐀𝐄: 𝐃𝐢𝐠𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐩𝐞𝐮𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐬 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐏𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐭 𝐍𝐞𝐞𝐝𝐬. 👥 ~1,300 participants. Two intense days with many discussions and even more questions. 𝐀𝐭 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐜𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐫 𝐨𝐟 𝐢𝐭 𝐚𝐥𝐥 𝐰𝐚𝐬 𝐨𝐧𝐞 𝐜𝐫𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐪𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧: How should healthcare respond to people using AI for mental health challenges — especially when vulnerable users are involved? The conversation highlighted three critical points: 🧠 𝐀𝐈 𝐥𝐚𝐜𝐤𝐬 𝐡𝐮𝐦𝐚𝐧 𝐜𝐨𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐱𝐭 Our current Generative AI models are limited in supporting vulnerable patients seeking comfort or advice and are not designed to replace human empathy or clinical judgment. As adoption grows, we must strengthen public understanding of what AI can - and cannot - responsibly provide. 📊 𝐄𝐯𝐢𝐝𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐟𝐢𝐫𝐬𝐭 Digital innovation creates value only when grounded in clinical validation, aligned with health system priorities and focused on meaningful outcomes. Frameworks like Germany’s DiGA show how regulation and reimbursement can enable responsible, scalable adoption of digital therapeutics. 🤝 𝐈𝐧𝐭𝐞𝐠𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐨𝐯𝐞𝐫 𝐫𝐞𝐬𝐢𝐬𝐭𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞. Patients turn to AI because they want fast answers and accessible guidance. Instead of ignoring this reality, we need closer collaboration among healthcare stakeholders to integrate digital tools responsibly into care pathways. AI is already part of the patient journey. The real question is how we shape its role safely, ethically and evidence-based. ➡️ What would you like AI to be better at? Thanks you Dr. Nahida Nayaz Ahmed , Dr Zain Al Yafei and Sakina for the collaboration and the organization of a great event. #Sakina #DigitalHealth #DigitalTherapeutics #MentalHealth #DiGA #HealthcareInnovation #GlobalHealth ...more

Two days ago, the new #SchillingReport2026 was published showing that executive leadership teams are getting older. The average age of executive leadership teams is now 53 years, and still primarily male. Yesterday, 𝐒𝐑𝐅 𝐍𝐞𝐰𝐬 program 𝟏𝟎𝐯𝐨𝐫𝟏𝟎 — one of Switzerland’s leading late-evening news programs with strong national reach — reached out to our Executive MBA Digital Leadership HWZ to comment and share our perspectives. The perfect opportunity to put our learnings from the EMBA into practice (including perfoming with very limited preparation time 😅). Here are my key reflections on the report: 🎯 There is no substitute for 𝐥𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐝 𝐞𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞. We often learn more from failures than from successes, and age can be a proxy for experience. In an increasingly complex world, experience does makes a difference. 🧠 But the world is not only becoming 𝐦𝐨𝐫𝐞 𝐜𝐨𝐦𝐩𝐥𝐞𝐱, it is 𝐞𝐯𝐨𝐥𝐯𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐟𝐚𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐫 than ever. With the accelerating pace of disruptive technologies, different leadership profiles are needed to succeed in the future. 🧩 While Switzerland still needs to catch up on “traditional” diversity such as generational and gender diversity, I believe leadership teams in this new world require even more: • 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐞𝐫𝐢𝐞𝐧𝐜𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲: Varied professional and life experiences across industries and roles. • 𝐂𝐨𝐠𝐧𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲: Different ways of thinking and problem-solving. • 𝐂𝐮𝐥𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐥 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐬𝐨𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥 𝐝𝐢𝐯𝐞𝐫𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐲: Multiple nationalities, languages, and socio-economic perspectives to foster inclusive innovation. But I’m even more curious: What would you have said? Are our executive teams too old? Do we need more diverse, younger perspectives or are other aspects more important? ---------------------------------------- Links to the Schilling and SRF report is in the comments. #Leadership #Diversity #ExperienceMatters #GenerationalDiversity #CognitiveDiversity #CulturalDiversity #FutureOfWork #DigitalLeadership #EMBA ...more

I’m excited to be invited as a speaker at #𝐒𝐈𝐌𝐂𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 – the Sakina Integrated Mental Health Conference in 𝐀𝐛𝐮 𝐃𝐡𝐚𝐛𝐢 this week, where I’ll be presenting on: 𝙍𝙚𝙞𝙢𝙖𝙜𝙞𝙣𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙈𝙚𝙣𝙩𝙖𝙡 𝙃𝙚𝙖𝙡𝙩𝙝 𝘾𝙖𝙧𝙚 𝙞𝙣 𝙩𝙝𝙚 𝙐𝘼𝙀: 𝘿𝙞𝙜𝙞𝙩𝙖𝙡 𝙏𝙝𝙚𝙧𝙖𝙥𝙚𝙪𝙩𝙞𝙘𝙨 𝙛𝙤𝙧 𝘾𝙝𝙖𝙣𝙜𝙞𝙣𝙜 𝙋𝙖𝙩𝙞𝙚𝙣𝙩 𝙉𝙚𝙚𝙙𝙨 Working in a global role gives me a unique perspective on how different health systems approach mental health — what works, what doesn’t, and how digital innovation can help bridge gaps in access, quality, and personalization of care. Together with Daria Radant , we’ll provide an overview of digital health and digital therapeutics, sharing real-world insights on how these solutions can support evolving patient needs. We’ll also take a deeper dive into how Germany’s DiGA framework has set a global benchmark for evidence-based, regulated, and reimbursed digital therapeutics. Four intense and incredibly enriching weeks are behind me — and the TEDx Talk was only one part of it. 😄 Earlier this year, I began my journey in the 𝗘𝘅𝗲𝗰𝘂𝘁𝗶𝘃𝗲 𝗠𝗕𝗔 𝗶𝗻 𝗗𝗶𝗴𝗶𝘁𝗮𝗹 𝗟𝗲𝗮𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗵𝗶𝗽, a 16-month program dedicated to navigating technological change and shaping the future of leadership. At the end of October, I headed to 𝗕𝗼𝘀𝘁𝗼𝗻 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗡𝗲𝘄 𝗬𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗮 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆 𝗧𝗼𝘂𝗿 exploring how AI is transforming industries and shaping better decision-making. I don’t think I’ve ever asked so many questions in one week. 😅 Here are a few reflections from selected visits: 💡 Swissnex in Boston and New York ( Brendan Karch ) reminded us that innovation only matters when wrapped in context and human relevance - and why storytelling is strategic infrastructure in the age of AI. 🧬 In predictive biology, Lakshmi Kuttippurathu, Ph.D highlighted how AI accelerates discovery in identifying therapeutic target. Key learning: Leadership means understanding where technology can guide humans, and where humans must guide technology. 📈 Aldo Luevano , CEO of a leading AI company in Latin America challenged us to go "ROI first, not AI first". Successful AI adoption begins with value creation, measurable impact, and the discipline to deliver results within months, not years. 🧠 At Microsoft , anthropologist Mary Gray prompted us to think where NOT to use AI and emphasized where humans outperform AI: ambiguity, context, and social intelligence. Researcher Zana Buçinca showed how AI can lead to overreliance and de-skilling and why we must build AI systems that enhance thinking, not replace it. 🤖 At Meta ( Gabriel Perlman , Aisha Iqbal), we discussed Meta's ambition for “personal superintelligence.” It’s a bold vision that raises important questions about personalization, data use, and societal benefit. Ultimately, leaders must ask not only what AI can do, but who it truly serves. 📰 With Erin Delmore , a BBC news reporter, we explored how AI fuels an information crisis. Curated, trusted news becomes even more vital as fake/ misleading content rises. Leaders must treat information quality as a strategic priority. 💳 And at Mastercard ( Chantal Ricketts , Jian Bland ), one insight stood out: about 85% of the skills needed in 2030 do not exist today. AI is reshaping work at a pace few organizations are prepared for — and leadership must evolve just as quickly 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗦𝘁𝘂𝗱𝘆 𝗧𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗺𝗮𝗱𝗲 𝗼𝗻𝗲 𝘁𝗿𝘂𝘁𝗵 𝗰𝗹𝗲𝗮𝗿: AI is not replacing leaders; it is demanding better ones. Those who will thrive are not the ones who adopt AI fastest, but those who ask harder questions - about value, context, ethics, and human capability. Groeneveld for organizing these incredible encounters and leading our Study Tour — and to all my study colleagues for all the shared moments! ...more

Ein Alarmsystem für 200'000 Franken. Zum Schutz vor Gewalt. Gebraucht hat es im Ernstfall noch nie jemand. Nicht, weil nichts passiert. Sondern weil niemand genau weiss, ob und wann er den Knopf drücken darf, wer dann kommt und was dann und danach geschieht. Eine Massnahme ohne eingebettete Handlungskompetenz erzeugt keine Sicherheit. Sie erzeugt die Illusion davon. Warum Gewaltprävention eine Führungsaufgabe ist und nicht bloss eine Frage der Ausstattung, findest du in meinem Artikel in der aktuellen Ausgabe von HR Today .
activity.text_en: An alarm system for 200,000 francs. To protect against violence. No one has ever needed it in an emergency. Not because nothing happens. But because no one knows exactly whether and when they can press the button, who will come and what will happen then and after. A measure without embedded competence to act does not create any security. It creates the illusion of it. You can find out why violence prevention is a management task and not just a question of equipment in my article in the current issue of HR Today .

activity.text: I'm pleased to share that I have stepped into the role of Country Head of Takeda Switzerland, as part of our new Central Europe Cluster. Before saying anything about what's ahead, a genuine thank you to the team of our Oncology, Rare Diseases and Plasma-Derived Therapies Business Unit for the past two years of delivery, trust and shared purpose, and to the leaders and colleagues who supported me along the way. The way this team shows up for patients, and for each other, is the reason I'm energised to take on what comes next. Takeda Switzerland is entering a new chapter, moving into a more focused, connected and customer-oriented way of working, aligned across the Central Europe Cluster and the wider IBU. This is about becoming a simpler, faster organisation that can continue delivering on our commitment to patients across our therapeutic areas. My focus for the coming months is straightforward: protect momentum on our portfolio through the transformation, make the cluster collaboration work in practice, and lead with transparency and fairness so our team can do their best work. I'll always come back to the same compass question: what's best for patients? Looking forward to leading this next chapter alongside an exceptional Swiss team and our colleagues across the Cluster and the IBU. #Takeda #NewChapter #PatientsFirst

Spannender Austausch heute am #SHQA FFI AI Forum in Rotkreuz – vielen Dank an Corinne Wild (PhD, CMD) und Patrick Fischer für die Möglichkeit, die Perspektive der Patientenorganisationen einzubringen. Viele Patientenorganisationen in der Schweiz werden von Betroffenen oder Angehörigen geführt - meist im Ehrenamt und ohne verlässliche strukturelle Finanzierung. Und das, obwohl sie im Rahmen nationaler Programme wie der Strategie Seltene Krankheiten, der NCD-Strategie und dem Nationalen Krebsplan klare Aufgaben übernehmen. Hier entsteht eine deutliche Lücke zwischen Erwartung und Realität. AI (KI) kann heute schon helfen, diese zu überbrücken, z.B. ermöglicht sie professionelle, konsistente Kommunikation - auch mehrsprachig - und hilft, Inputs aus der Medizin effizient zu strukturieren und nutzbar zu machen. Aber es ginge noch mehr: AI kann helfen, gelebte Erfahrung in etwas zu überführen, das vergleichbar, transparent, methodisch fundiert und für HTA-Entscheidungen nutzbar ist. Wenn wir das richtig nutzen, ist AI ein echter Enabler. Und genau das brauchen wir!
activity.text_en: Exciting exchange today at the #SHQA FFI AI Forum in Rotkreuz – many thanks to Corinne Wild (PhD, CMD) and Patrick Fischer for the opportunity to contribute the perspective of the patient organisations. Many patient organisations in Switzerland are run by sufferers or relatives - mostly on a voluntary basis and without reliable structural funding. And this despite the fact that they take on clear tasks within the framework of national programmes such as the Rare Diseases Strategy, the NCD Strategy and the National Cancer Plan. This creates a clear gap between expectation and reality. AI (AI) can already help to bridge these today, e.g. enables professional, consistent communication - including multilingual communication - and helps to efficiently structure and make use of inputs from medicine. But there is more: AI can help transform lived experience into something that is comparable, transparent, methodologically sound and usable for HTA decisions. If we use that correctly, AI is a real enabler. And that's exactly what we need!

activity.text: Yesterday at bio:cap : Can Europe truly own the future of biomedical AI? My answer: Yes! But not in the way you might expect.💡 Europe will not win this race only through scale. Our advantage lies in the ability to integrate innovation into regulated, evidence-based care. Not the fastest AI model wins. In the longrung, the most clinically robust and trusted one does. One thought that stays with me: patients are already using consumer AI today, with or without us. So the real question is not whether we enable AI in healthcare. It is how. Within a safe, regulated framework – or outside of it. My three takeaways from the panel: 1. Regulation is not a barrier! It is our competitive advantage. The DiGA framework proves it: evidence, reimbursement, and real-world implementation can go hand in hand. What we need now are faster, iterative approval processes, so that good solutions reach patients without unnecessary delay. 2. Scaling remains the unfinished homework! DiGA demonstrate Germany's early-mover advantage in reimbursed digital innovation. For Europe, this means: we need harmonized frameworks that give verified innovations the systemic reach they deserve. 3. Human-centered AI means the right technology, at the right moment, embedded in real care pathways. Not consumer AI, but safe, reimbursed, outcomes-driven digital therapies that close gaps in care for physicians and patients. That is Europe's true AI identity. Thank you Daniel Rettig for the excellent moderation – and to Saila Rinne, Markus Vogel and Dr. Sievert Weiss for the different perspectives that made this panel so relevant. NEXT Pharma Summit — Conference Synthesis & Reflections Two days. Seventeen sessions. Thirty-plus speakers from competing companies. One diagnosis, arrived at independently, repeatedly, from every angle. The industry knows what good looks like. It just can't seem to build it. The problem is not insight. Every challenge was named clearly across both days — incentive design, behavioural science gaps, trust deficits, upstream decision-makers, systems lagging behind science. The problem is not technology. The tools exist: AI-assisted diagnosis, MLR automation, LLM narrative tracking, cross-functional orchestration platforms. The gap is the architecture. The cross-functional operating model. The shared KPIs that survive a leadership change. The implementation design that scales a validated pilot without losing what made it work. The feedback loop that brings field signal back into strategy in time to matter. This is what Iroda Jurabekova meant across both days: we are launching tomorrow's science into yesterday's systems. It's what Cristina Finazzi meant when she said trust cannot be downloaded. It's what Dr. Eve Huber meant when she said AI is a multiplier of your system, not a fixer of it. The patient is the test that cuts through every argument. Run any organisational design question through what the patient actually needs and the right answer arrives faster than any alignment process. At Crackle Health, this is the work we do. We build the connective tissue — the cross-functional frameworks, the implementation architecture, the operating models that make insight actionable and transformation real rather than tracked. If you left Dubrovnik with the same feeling I did — diagnosis clear, gap in the building — I'd like to talk. Not a sales call. A conversation please reach out. Longer form article will follow. #NEXTPharma #Pharma #DigitalHealth #HCPEngagement #PatientOutcomes #CrackleHealth

As mental health awareness month draws to a close, I volunteered to moderate a panel during the #AFN Impact stage held at the Zurich Kunsthaus on Friday 29 May. The panel dicussion - Breaking Silence: A Dialogue on Mental Health in the African Community in Switzerland, brought together clinicians, therapists, and a fashion designer with lived experience for an honest and much-needed conversation. Throughout the evening, we explored the impact of depression, trauma, migration, loneliness, discrimination, parenting, and belonging on mental health. One message resonated across every perspective shared: Connection matters, and seeking help early matters even more. Many people struggle in silence, often waiting until they reach a crisis before reaching out for support. Our panel emphasized that mental health challenges rarely appear overnight—they often develop gradually and can be addressed more effectively when recognized early. The discussion provided practical advice for participants: 🔹 Build and maintain meaningful social connections 🔹 Pay attention to early signs of emotional distress in yourself and your loved ones 🔹 Create safe spaces for conversations at home and in our communities 🔹 Seek professional support early—whether through therapy, counselling, or medical care 🔹 Remember that asking for help is a sign of strength, not weakness Thank you to our panelists, Dr. med. Philipp K. M. Katumba , Jânia Morgado Silva , Dr. med. Fana Asefaw , Belinda Kakanou , Safiétou Seck , Andrea Moser for your kind assistance, all the attendees, and everyone who contributed to a thoughtful and impactful dialogue. The conversation does not end here. Together, we can continue to reduce stigma, strengthen community support, and ensure that no one feels they have to face mental health challenges alone. #MentalHealth #BreakingSilence #AfricanDiaspora #MentalHealthAwareness #CommunityWellbeing #Zurich #Switzerland #AFN
